lesson.title: The alternator: a turning field makes three phases

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each coil's wave making one cycle for each pole pair that sweeps past it, a north pole and then a south, when you turn the rotor round.
interactive.title: The turning field
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Six show an idea and seven ask you to try it. No marks and no timers.

The picture. On the left is a cross-section of an alternator. The stator is the fixed outer ring. It carries coils marked A, B and C. The rotor turns inside it, with its poles marked N and S. Field arrows run out of each north pole and round into the next south pole. The rotor wears a ring to drag it round by. On the screens where you drag it, a Rotor position slider turns it too. A Play button spins it. A pole switch of three buttons gives 2, 4 or 6 poles. With 2 poles the stator carries one set of three coils, A, B and C, 120° apart. With 4 poles it carries two sets, A, B, C, A, B, C, 60° apart. With 6 poles it carries three sets, 40° apart. So each set of three spans one pole pair. Each phase's coils are joined in series. A coil glows while its flux changes fastest, as the gap between two poles passes it. On the right, three traces labelled A, B and C are drawn against time as the rotor turns, one for each phase. Each trace is one coil's voltage. A dashed line marked full field shows where each wave peaks at full field and 60 Hz. A speed slider sets the rotor's speed, from 0 to 3600 rev/min in steps of 60. A field-current slider sets the current in the rotor's winding as a percentage of full field. It runs from 0 to 120% in steps of 10. The picture runs 60 times slower than real, so you can follow it. At 1800 rev/min one turn takes 2 s on screen.

The readouts sit in four tiles: Pole pairs, Speed in rev/min, Frequency in Hz and Voltage between lines in V. Two screens leave the Voltage tile out. On a phone the tiles wrap onto two rows. The three pole buttons wrap too.

The rule it computes. Each pole pair sweeping past a coil makes one cycle. The rotor turns rev/min ÷ 60 times a second. So frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. Each phase's voltage follows E = 4.44 f N Φ. The turns N are fixed, and the flux Φ is in proportion to the field current. Each pole setting stands for a machine built to make 440 V between lines at 60 Hz on full field. So voltage = 440 × (frequency ÷ 60) × (field current ÷ 100%). Each trace's height follows it. At 4 poles, 1800 rev/min and full field, the readouts give 2 pole pairs, 60 Hz and 440 V. With the rotor stopped, or the field current at 0, the traces run flat.

Screen 1, try it, a recall. 2 poles at 1800 rev/min, coil A only, with its trace and the tiles hidden until Check. "A coil spins steadily in a magnet's field and makes an AC wave. Now it spins twice as fast. What happens to its wave?" Three choices, in this order: "Just as tall, but each cycle takes half the time"; "Twice as tall, and each cycle takes half the time"; "Twice as tall, with cycles as long as before". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The flux now changes twice as fast as well. So the coil makes more voltage, not just quicker cycles." Hint for the third: "Each turn makes one cycle. Twice the turns a second means each cycle takes half the time." Why: "Each turn makes one cycle. So twice the speed packs twice the cycles into each second, and each takes half the time. The flux through the coil also changes twice as fast. So the wave stands twice as tall. Speed moves both together. The alternator here does the same, with the magnet turning instead of the coil." A right Check says "Still there." Then the rotor spins, and partway through its speed doubles from 1800 to 3600 rev/min. Coil A's wave grows twice as tall, and its cycles come twice as often. Read: the question.

Screen 2, show. 2 poles, full field, coil A only; B and C are drawn faint. The words: "An alternator is the turning-coil generator turned inside out. Its coils stay still in the stator, the fixed outer ring. So the big output currents leave through fixed connections. The rotor turns inside. Only a small direct current crosses onto it, to make it a magnet with a north and a south pole. Drag the rotor round once. Coil A's flux rises as the north pole arrives and falls as it leaves. Then the south pole sends flux through the other way. One turn makes one full cycle." Read: "The rotor is a magnet with one north and one south pole. It turns inside the fixed stator. The coils stay still, so the big output currents leave through fixed connections. As the north pole and then the south pole pass coil A, its trace makes one full cycle. That happens once every turn." Still: the rotor dragged one full turn, coil A's trace drawn for that turn.

Screen 3, try it. "The rotor stops with its north pole square in front of coil A. The field current is still on. What voltage does coil A make?" Three choices, in this order: "Its biggest, because the flux through it is strongest"; "A steady direct voltage, because the field current is direct"; "None, because the flux through it is not changing". Right, the third. Hint for the first: "Voltage comes from the flux changing, not from how much there is. A parked pole changes nothing." Hint for the second: "The rotor's current is direct. But a coil only gets a voltage while a pole moves past it." Why: "A coil makes voltage only while the flux through it changes. A parked pole gives coil A plenty of flux, but the flux is steady. So coil A makes nothing until the rotor turns again." A right Check shows coil A's trace lying flat at zero. Read: "The rotor stops with its north pole square in front of coil A. The field current is still on. What voltage does coil A make?"

Screen 4, show. 2 poles at 3600 rev/min, full field, all three coils. The words: "Now add coils B and C. Each sits 120° round the stator from the last. Tap Play. The north pole reaches B a third of a turn after A. It reaches C a third of a turn after that. So the three waves have the same shape, each 120° behind the last. These are the three phases you already know, and here is their cause. Each coil is one phase's winding. A coil lights up while its flux changes fastest, as the gap between two poles passes it." Read: "Coils B and C sit 120° round the stator from A and from each other. Each pole reaches them a third of a turn later. So three equal waves build, each 120° behind the one before. Each coil lights up as the gap between two poles passes it, where its flux changes fastest." Still: playing, a turn and a half of all three traces drawn.

Screen 5, try it, typed. The Voltage tile is left out. "A 2-pole rotor turns at 3000 rev/min. Coil B sits 120° on from coil A, in the direction the rotor turns. How long after coil A's wave peaks does coil B's wave peak?" A field in ms. Answer 6.67 ms. Slips: 20 ms, "That is a whole turn. B is only a third of a turn on from A."; 13.33 ms, "That is two thirds of a turn, from B on round to A. The rotor reaches B first."; 3.33 ms, "That is a sixth of a turn. 120° is a third of 360°." Hint when wrong: "Work out how long one turn takes. Then take a third of it." Why: "3000 rev/min is 3000 ÷ 60 = 50 turns a second. So one turn takes 1 ÷ 50 s, which is 20 ms. Coil B is a third of a turn on. So its wave peaks 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 ms after A's." Read: "A 2-pole rotor turns at 3000 rev/min. Coil B sits 120° on from coil A, in the direction the rotor turns. How long after coil A's wave peaks does coil B's wave peak?"

Screen 6, show. 4 poles, full field, the rotor at rest for dragging. The words: "Now the rotor has 4 poles: north, south, north, south. Drag it round once. Coil A now sees a north and a south go by twice. So it makes two full cycles in one turn. A north and a south together are a pole pair. Each pole pair that passes makes one cycle. So the stator carries a set of three coils for each pole pair. A pole pair passes in half a turn. A third of that is 60° of rotor, and 120° of wave." Read: "A 4-pole rotor has two pole pairs. Coil A sees a north and a south go by twice each turn. So it makes two full cycles a turn. The stator carries a set of three coils for each pole pair, 60° apart. A pole pair passes in half a turn, so 60° of rotor is 120° of wave." Still: 4 poles, the rotor dragged one turn, two cycles on each trace.

Screen 7, try it, typed. 6 poles at 1200 rev/min, with the tiles hidden until Check. "A 6-pole rotor makes one full turn. How many full cycles does coil A make?" A field in cycles. Answer 3 cycles. Slips: 6, "That counts poles. A cycle needs a north and a south, so count pole pairs."; 1, "One cycle a turn is the 2-pole machine only. Each pole pair gives one cycle." Hint when wrong: "Pair each north pole with a south pole. Then count the pairs." Why: "6 poles make 3 pole pairs, each a north and a south. Each pair sweeping past coil A makes one cycle. So one turn makes 3." A right Check draws one turn: three cycles on each trace. Read: "A 6-pole rotor makes one full turn. How many full cycles does coil A make?"

Screen 8, show. 4 poles at 1800 rev/min, full field, with the speed slider and pole switch free. The words: "The rotor turns rev/min ÷ 60 times a second. Each turn gives one cycle for each pole pair. So frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. A 2-pole machine must turn at 3600 rev/min to make 60 Hz.[^1] A 4-pole one needs only 1800 rev/min. The rule is printed two ways. f = P × n ÷ 60 counts P in pole pairs. f = P × N ÷ 120 counts P in poles. Always check which P you have." Read: "Frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. A 2-pole machine makes 60 Hz at 3600 rev/min. A 4-pole one makes it at 1800 rev/min. The rule is also printed as f = P × N ÷ 120, where P counts poles." Still: 4 poles, 1800 rev/min, 60 Hz.

Screen 9, try it, typed. The tiles for pole pairs, frequency and voltage read ? until Check. "A 4-pole set turns at 1800 rev/min. What frequency does it make?" A field in Hz. Answer 60 Hz. Slips: 120 Hz, "4 poles are 2 pole pairs. That answer puts poles into the pole-pair form."; 30 Hz, "The form with 120 counts poles, so 4 goes in, not 2." Hint when wrong: "Count the pole pairs first." Why: "4 poles make 2 pole pairs. So 2 × 1800 ÷ 60 = 60 Hz. The poles form gives 4 × 1800 ÷ 120 = 60 Hz. Both forms agree when P means what each one says." A right Check sets the picture to 4 poles at 1800 rev/min. Read: "A 4-pole set turns at 1800 rev/min. What frequency does it make?"

Screen 10, show. 4 poles, with the speed slider opening at 1710 rev/min and the field-current slider at 100%, both free. The words: "Each coil's voltage follows the transformer rule, E = 4.44 f N Φ. Its turns N were fixed when it was wound. The speed sets f, so it moves the voltage too. The field current sets the flux Φ, so it moves only the voltage. Say a 4-pole set with nothing connected makes 440 V at 60 Hz. Slow it 5%, to 1710 rev/min. It makes 57 Hz and 418 V. Put the speed back and turn the field current down instead. The waves shrink, but they come just as often." Read: "Take a 4-pole set with nothing connected and the field unchanged. Slowed 5%, from 1800 to 1710 rev/min, its waves get both lower and less frequent: 57 Hz and 418 V. Turning the field current down shrinks the waves but leaves them at 60 Hz." Still: 4 poles, 1710 rev/min, full field.

Screen 11, try it. "A set running alone on its board reads 58 Hz. What brings it back to 60 Hz?" Three choices, in this order: "Raising the field current"; "Speeding up the engine"; "Either one, since both change the waves". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The field current changes the flux, and so the height of the waves. Only poles passing more often raises the frequency." Hint for the third: "Speed moves both. The field current moves the voltage only." Why: "Frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. The field is nowhere in that rule. So only the speed changes the frequency. The voltage comes back up with the speed." A right Check slides the speed up until the frequency reads 60 Hz. Read: "A set running alone on its board reads 58 Hz. What brings it back to 60 Hz?"

Screen 12, try it, typed (mixed). "A 6-pole set with nothing connected makes 440 V at 60 Hz. Its engine slows to 1080 rev/min. The field current stays the same. What voltage does it make now?" A field in V. Answer 396 V. Slips: 440 V, "The field is unchanged, but the poles now pass less often. So the flux changes more slowly."; 489 V, "That ratio is upside down. A lower frequency gives a lower voltage."; 792 V, "6 poles are 3 pole pairs, not 6." Hint when wrong: "Find the new frequency first. Then scale 440 V by it." Why: "6 poles are 3 pole pairs. So the frequency is 3 × 1080 ÷ 60 = 54 Hz. With the field unchanged, the voltage falls in step: 440 × 54 ÷ 60 = 396 V." Read: "A 6-pole set with nothing connected makes 440 V at 60 Hz. Its engine slows to 1080 rev/min. The field current stays the same. What voltage does it make now?"

Screen 13, try it, typed (mixed). The Voltage tile is left out. "What speed must a 6-pole alternator turn at to make 50 Hz?" A field in rev/min. Answer 1000 rev/min. Slips: 500 rev/min, "That counts 6 pole pairs. 6 poles are 3 pairs."; 2000 rev/min, "The form with 120 counts poles, so 6 goes in, not 3." Hint when wrong: "Turn the rule round: rev/min = frequency × 60 ÷ pole pairs." Why: "6 poles are 3 pole pairs. So rev/min = 50 × 60 ÷ 3 = 1000. As a check, 3 × 1000 ÷ 60 = 50 Hz." A right Check sets the picture to 6 poles at 1000 rev/min, and a closing line reads: "Speed sets the frequency. The field current sets the voltage. Next comes the regulator that trims the field." Read: "What speed must a 6-pole alternator turn at to make 50 Hz?"
interactive.ignores: The picture runs 60 times slower than real. Its waves are drawn as perfect sines. A real machine's waves are close to sines, but not exact. Each pole setting stands for a different machine built to make 440 V at 60 Hz on full field. That is because a real machine's poles are fixed when it is built. The speed slider runs well past what a 4- or 6-pole set is built for, so the rule can be seen. Real sets run near their rated speed. The flux is drawn in proportion to the field current. Real iron saturates, so more field current adds less and less flux. With no field current, the iron's leftover magnetism still makes a small voltage. Nothing is connected, so no current flows and nothing loads the engine. The picture leaves out how the field current reaches the turning rotor. Some small machines turn their coils inside a fixed magnet instead. Real stator coils are spread across many slots. That trims the 4.44 by a factor near 1, called the winding factor.

explain.text:
A generator set's alternator is a magnet turning inside fixed coils.[^3] A north pole and then a south pole sweep past each coil. That makes one full cycle of voltage in it. Three coils spaced round the magnet make three waves 120° apart.[^2] These are the three phases.

The fixed outer part is the [[stator]], and it carries the coils. The turning part is the [[rotor]]. Direct current in the rotor's winding makes it an electromagnet. Its poles do not change. The engine turns the rotor, and its field turns with it. As a north pole comes up to a coil, more of its flux passes through the coil. As the pole moves on, that flux falls away. Then a south pole sends flux through the other way. A coil makes voltage only while the flux through it changes, just as in a transformer. So a pole parked in front of a coil makes nothing, however strong it is. A north and a south passing make one full cycle. On a 2-pole machine, coils B and C sit 120° round the stator from coil A. They see the same poles a third of a turn later. So their waves have the same shape, each 120° behind the last.

A rotor can carry more than one north and one south. A north and a south together make a [[pole pair]]. Each pole pair sweeping past a coil makes one cycle. So a 4-pole rotor makes two cycles in each coil every turn. Its stator carries a set of three coils for each pole pair. That keeps the three phases 120° apart in the wave. The rotor turns rev/min ÷ 60 times a second. So frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. A 2-pole machine has one pole pair. It must turn at 3600 rev/min to make 60 Hz.[^1] A 4-pole machine makes 60 Hz at 1800 rev/min, and 50 Hz at 1500. The rule is printed two ways. f = P × n ÷ 60 counts P in pole pairs. f = P × N ÷ 120 counts P in poles. A motor's synchronous speed rule, ns = 120 f ÷ p, is the second one turned round. Put poles into the pole-pair form and the answer doubles.

Each phase's voltage follows the transformer rule, E = 4.44 f N Φ. Its turns N are fixed when it is wound. The frequency f comes from the speed. The flux Φ comes from the field current. Take a set running alone with nothing connected. A change of speed moves the frequency and the voltage together. A change of field current moves the voltage alone. It changes the flux, but not how often the poles pass. Say a 4-pole set makes 440 V at 60 Hz at 1800 rev/min. Slow it 5% to 1710 rev/min, with the field unchanged. It now makes 2 × 1710 ÷ 60 = 57 Hz. Its voltage is 440 × 57 ÷ 60 = 418 V. This is a simple picture of a machine with nothing connected. In a real one, the iron limits how far more field current raises the flux. The load pulls the voltage about too. Paralleling comes down to these two handles: the engine's fuel and the field current. Paralleling asks what each one does when two sets share one board. **A field turning past fixed coils makes three phases 120° apart. Each pole pair that passes makes one cycle, so the frequency is locked to the speed. The field current changes the voltage the coils make, not the frequency.**

analogy.text: Picture a toothed wheel turning past a sensor. The sensor clicks once as each tooth goes by. Clicks a second = teeth × rev/min ÷ 60. So a wheel with twice the teeth clicks twice as often at the same speed. The rotor is that wheel, with a pole pair for each tooth. Each coil is a sensor.
analogy.breaks: One tooth makes a click, but it takes a north and a south pole to make one cycle. That is exactly where the poles-or-pole-pairs slip comes from. And a counter counts each click once, whatever its size. A coil's voltage is more than a count. It grows with the speed and with the field current.

practice.text:
**Safety first:** treat a turning alternator as live, even with its breaker open. Its coils make a voltage whenever a magnetised rotor sweeps past them.

- Read the number of poles off the plate. Or work it out from the rated speed and frequency.
- Halve it to get the pole pairs.
- Frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. Turned round, rev/min = frequency × 60 ÷ pole pairs.
- If a printed formula has 120 in it, its P counts poles. If it has 60, its P counts pole pairs.
- Take a set running alone, with nothing connected and the field current unchanged. Its voltage moves in proportion to the frequency.

**Rule of thumb:** poles × rev/min = 120 × frequency. For 60 Hz that is 7200. So 2, 4 and 6 poles turn at 3600, 1800 and 1200 rev/min. For 50 Hz it is 6000, so they turn at 3000, 1500 and 1000 rev/min.

**Worked example:** a set's plate reads 6 poles, 440 V, 60 Hz. It has 3 pole pairs, so it turns at 60 × 60 ÷ 3 = 1200 rev/min. Say its engine runs 2% slow, at 1176 rev/min, with the field unchanged. It makes 3 × 1176 ÷ 60 = 58.8 Hz. Its voltage is 440 × 58.8 ÷ 60 = 431.2 V. Raising the field current would bring the voltage back. Only the speed brings back 60 Hz.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting poles into the pole-pair form. That doubles the frequency. A 4-pole set at 1800 rev/min makes 60 Hz, not 120 Hz.
- Putting pole pairs into the poles form. That halves it, to 30 Hz.
- Reaching for the field current to correct the frequency. It changes the voltage the coils make, not the frequency.
- Expecting a strong field to make a voltage on its own. The flux through a coil must change, so the rotor must turn.

applied.problem: Two lines fail after i6: in parallel the handle is the engine's fuel, not its speed, which the board holds; and there the field current moves kVAr while the board voltage barely changes, so 'changes only the voltage' should say what it never changes: the frequency.

'It moves the voltage only' is unqualified in the dossier, but in parallel (i6) more field moves kVAr while the board voltage barely changes; the true, general point is that it changes the coils' voltage, not the frequency.

Screens 9 and 11 state voltage tracking frequency exactly, which holds only with nothing connected and the field unchanged (the explanation says so); and a set's 440 V is its line voltage, not each phase's E = 4.44 f N Φ.

notes.problem: The speed slider steps 60 rev/min, so screen 9's opening 1710 rev/min and screen 12's 1000 rev/min are not slider positions (they snap to 1680/1740 and 960/1020); the build must set those speeds exactly or use a finer step, else the readouts will not show 57 Hz/418 V or 50 Hz.
